results.title: True pricing – guiding consumers within a new pricing paradigm
results.content: Here, we present the results of a large-scale survey experiment with 1400 Dutch and Danish consumers, investigating the effect of the true price presentation format (absolute, relative or no information) on consumers’ choices. In specific, we investigate the effect of different price presentation formats on consumers’ choices accounting for consumers’ price-quality schema and understanding of true pricing. For true pricing to support consumers in making more sustainable choices at the point of sale, the information provided must at least be easy and fast to comprehend. Evidence from the existing market trials at Penny or Albert Heijn suggests that when hidden costs are communicated as absolute price premiums, it increases consumers’ focus on the overall true price and the sense that products are generally becoming more expensive (Stein et al., 2024. Journal of Marketing Research, 30(2), 234–245.")), consumers’ price quality schema was measured based on the level of agreement with four items on a 7-point Likert scale after the choice experiment.

results.title: Time warp: How marketers express time can affect what ...
results.content: According to new research from the UBC Sauder School of Business, the way time is expressed—as a calendar year or as a length of time—can change how people experience the past and the future, and influence real consumer decisions. "If the goal is to signal longevity, history or oldness, then you should use the number of years," said Dr. Deepak Sirwani, an associate professor in the marketing and behavioral science division and co-author of the study. Deepak Sirwani et al, EXPRESS: When 'Year' Feels near: How Year versus Length Framing Alters Time Perception and Consumer Decisions, *Journal of Marketing Research* (2025). Describing time as a length (e.g., "10 years") makes durations feel longer than expressing the same period as calendar years (e.g., "since 2016"), a phenomenon termed the "year-length effect." This framing influences consumer perceptions and willingness to pay, with length-based descriptions enhancing value for aged goods and year-based descriptions benefiting newer or used items.
